utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Where do we stand now, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do your honours wish me to make the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I just want to know where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The situation is, your Honour, that the witness that was to follow the witness that is presently giving testimony was Mr. Panzer from the Austrian police. Early this morning, his wife suffered what they have described as a circulatory collapse. I cannot assist your honours in what that condition is, but it is such that he had to return to Vienna immediately and he also has a three year old son that it was necessary for the witness to go home to look after, in view of his wife's condition. This will cause some disruption to the programme the Prosecution had in terms of its witnesses, because it was anticipated that having regard to the fact that Mr. Panzer would be dealing with a large number of documents, that it was unlikely that his testimony would have been completed by tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before we proceed further, let us have the appearances so that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May it please your Honour, my name is Niemann, and I appear with Mr. Turone, Mr. Waespi and Ms. Van Dusschoten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your honours, I am Ms. Residovic, Defence counsel for Zejnil Delalic and with me is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your honours, my name is Olujic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Mucic. With me is Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your honours. My name is Tom Moran and I appear with Salih Karabdic for Mr. Delic, and because of the change in the Prosecution's witness schedule, we are not blaming anyone, but Mr. Karabdic had to make a quick trip to the detention centre to get Mr. Delic to identify some documents. He may well be back before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey and I am here representing Esad Landzo. Mr. Ackerman is ill today but he should be well enough to return tomorrow. I just wanted to bring to the court's attention that you have excused the appearance of Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Niemann, you are welcome to continue what you were trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. At this stage we simply do not know when Mr. Panzer can return to The Hague, whether it be next week or some later stage, as we do not know what the condition of his wife will be and his personal circumstances in that respect. Your honours, we did make provision for an additional witness to be available to give testimony. In fact, it is a witness that I had intended to take in evidence-in-chief. That witness is a gentleman by the name of Mr. Branko Sudar. His name is on the witness list. I am not sure what the position is with respect to the Defence in terms of their readiness for me to lead that witness. I would have thought that possibly Mr. Navrat may take the rest of the day in terms of his testimony, and in view of the fact that some of the accused are not here, it may either require us to bring in those accused, if we are to call this witness. So far as I am concerned, I am prepared to take this witness next in line. I would have appreciated more time to speak to the witness, this has all happened very suddenly, so certainly if the Defence need more time tomorrow morning to prepare, then that would also suit the Prosecution, but if they do not and they are ready to proceed at ten, then we will make ourselves ready for that purpose as well should we need to call that witness at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was just going to suggest that perhaps after we have dealt with the witness this afternoon we could have a short adjournment so those of us on this side of the bar could discuss how we would like to deal with that and whether there is any view about that and report back to your honours after a short adjournment. I do not know whether that would be convenient to your honours. I see my learned friend Mr. Niemann nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is certainly convenient as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Tomorrow is the only day we have for these arrangements as we are not sitting on Friday, so let us see how you carry on today and tomorrow you can start some of this and you tell me how you can bring your next witness. Let us have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will swear the interpreter first. THE INTERPRETER (sworn) WOLFGANG NAVRAT (continued)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I must remind you that you are still under your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I pass the witness

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honour, Mr. Navrat, can you help me please about this question. Can you tell us, please, whether you either speak, understand or read any of the Serbo-Croat group of languages, that is Croatian, Bosnian or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, those are what you might refer to as foreign languages for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you speak any foreign languages at all apart from German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do my best with English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am not going to put you to the test Mr. Navrat, all right. I want to ask you now, please, about the importance of preparing documents which you were asked about yesterday briefly. During the process of carrying out a search and an arrest and so on, a number of official documents have to be produced by law; that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where are they to be produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By police officers, in other words records of what has taken place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help us about this, please? What do you as a police officer see as the purpose of preparing records of activities that you have carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean this in general terms, or does this question relate specifically to the search in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In general terms we are going to deal with to start off with please, Mr. Navrat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say as far as the search goes, the record and the report about a search, the inventory, and if something is found, an inventory, then you would also need an analysis report, those would be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would like to see whether you agree with the following propositions, please, Mr. Navrat. Would you agree that producing a record, for example, of a search or of an arrest is firstly to provide reliable -- a reliable and accurate record of what has taken place during the search or the arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And then having produced the report, would you agree that it would then enable others who have to check what has happened to have an accurate and reliable account upon which they can rely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And after others, other police officers, other officials, have dealt with those documents, it enables the court to be able to have an accurate and reliable piece of evidence upon which it in turn can rely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you sign a document, Mr. Navrat, what do you perceive as the purpose of you signing a document such as a Niederschrift or a Bericht?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the contents of the document is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And if the contents are incorrect, what is the purpose of your signature in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I sign should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let us look at it the other way round. If the information contained in documents which, for example, you sign is incorrect, would you agree that those who use the document afterwards will be basing their information and their judgments on inaccurate, unreliable information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And if the information contained in the document which is inaccurate information pertains to the most important bits of information, that makes the document pretty well worthless, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally speaking I could go along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just dealing with this short issue on the place that the Niederschrift forms within the chain of making documents, is the Niederschrift a document which is physically taken along to the search?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, and that is also as per the code of criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that the only document which is taken to the search for making a record of what happens at the search?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, one also takes along the search warrant to hand it over to the person concerned on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, but in terms of a document upon which things are then written, is the Niederschrift the only one upon which information is recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, no, because the officer who has been in the field is going to be drawing up a report and need not necessarily rely on the record, the Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So he writes nothing down and then goes back to the office and does his best to remember what it is he has recovered, does he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he needs to, he will take it along, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But where a Niederschrift is used, it is from that document that a report would be prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So if information is recorded by the searching officers on the Niederschrift which is incorrect information, the report which is prepared from it will be based on inaccurate information, will it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would assume so, if you want to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In turn, when those documents are placed before either an Austrian court or, as here, before the International Tribunal at The Hague, in terms of the process we discussed earlier, the court is faced with a document which contains inaccurate information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that was the case in this instance, but I would like to add that subsequently the officers go on working on the case and then improve matters in a document that would be drawn up at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No doubt. I would like now to ask you please, Mr. Navrat, about some of the evidence which you gave to us yesterday. Can I remind you please of this, you were asked yesterday about the folders that you had seized at the INDA-Bau building. You told their honours this: "I put these folders in a plastic bag and we put all the seized items together; that is to say I took these and the video tapes to the police station." You were then asked this question: "When you say police station, which police station is that? Answer: That is my department, that is in Vienna, in the 1st district, Schotenring 729, 3rd floor." You were then asked this question: "Where did you go in the building on the 3rd floor? Answer: In the department concerned, I believe it is room 326. Question: When you went into room 326, what did you do then? Answer: I handed over the box with the videos and the bag with the folders. I put those on Mr. Panzer's desk and I told him I was done with the search and then he took over these items for further processing." A few moments later, you told the court that the room in which Mr. Panzer was handed the folders was the room where Mr. Panzer and his team ordinarily worked. Do you recall giving us that evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want now to tell you about the evidence which Mr. Moerbaur gave to this Tribunal on Day 35, which was some time ago in June. First of all he told us that his team, that of Mr. Panzer, Mr. Moerbaur and Bycek, was room 331. He gave evidence that you came to room 331 and gave him the seized objects from INDA-Bau; that you gave Mr. Moerbaur the material after 5 pm, and that the INDA-Bau material was contained in boxes, and on the following day he told us this -- he was asked this question by Mr. Turone: "Going back to the afternoon of 18th March, you said that your colleague Navrat brought into room 331, materials seized in the premises of INDA-Bau right after the house search. Answer: Yes, Navrat on 18th March, in the afternoon, brought the objects to me in room 331 of the Vienna headquarters." Then a few pages further on, Mr. Turone asked this question: "Mr. Moerbaur, you say that amongst the seized material brought by Mr. Navrat and given to you by Mr. Navrat and coming from INDA-Bau, there were also 12 files? Answer: Yes, that is right." Mr. Navrat, do you see from what I have just read out to you that the two accounts that have been given to this Tribunal concerning these documents, these files, are completely different accounts; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please explain in a little bit more detail exactly where you see a contradiction? Which contradiction are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbaur says that you gave him the seized materials from INDA-Bau. You have told us that you gave them to Grupenfuhrer Panzer. They are not the same people, are they, Mr. Navrat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not necessarily see a contradiction in that, because apparently Mr. Moerbaur and Mr. Panzer were in the room at the time and Mr. Panzer as a superior would have been the one I would have addressed myself to but Mr. Moerbaur may have taken the things. I do not see a contradiction in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We will leave that for others to judge, Mr. Navrat. You told us you handed over a box with the videos and a bag with the folders. Mr. Moerbaur told us they were all in boxes. Do you see a contradiction between those pieces of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in a cardboard box, the video tapes, and I brought it into the office where Mr. Panzer and his people work and it was given to Mr. Panzer. I take it that Mr. Moerbaur was present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He has told us the material was brought in boxes, not that it was brought some in boxes and some in a bag.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plastic bag was probably inside that cardboard box.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just one small thing, you think that you do not know where room 331 is in the headquarters building, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to point out that there is over 120 people in our department and I do not know exactly -- I do not know each and every office number of each and every individual. Sometimes I do not even know my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It must make for a very confusing day at the office, Mr. Navrat. Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Esad Landzo's Defence counsel, I have no questions for this witness either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, nothing in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this is the end of his testimony. He is discharged. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your honours, I think that it might be useful if we could have a moment to have a discussion with members of the Defence in terms of proceeding with the next witness. We are in a position where we can proceed with a witness if all parties are happy for that to happen and obviously if that is convenient to the court. I think it might be useful if we could have a discussion first and then report back to your honours on our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think in the circumstances we will break for 30 minutes because then we might be able to determine what to do. We will break until 3.30.

procedural_notes.text: (Court adjourned until 10 am the following day)
